title: Proof pages for a restaurant group
metaTitle: Proof pages for a restaurant group
excerpt: A proof page should show the constraint, the decision, and the room with one dish. Pictures with no decision are decoration. End on the menu or a table for a similar guest.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall, a spare arrangement that still needs a reason before it can stand for a restaurant.
caption: Hangers on a branch, waiting for a reason. A restaurant page needs a reason too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is a proof page for a restaurant group?
faqs.answer: A page about one room or one change, told as a constraint, a decision, and the result: the room and one dish. It is not a photo reel and not a press release. A similar guest should be able to see the menu or book from the end of it.

faqs.question: Do guests read case studies?
faqs.answer: A guest deciding tonight will read a short proof if it helps them choose a room, and they will skip a monograph. Keep the page to one constraint and one dish, with the booking link in view. Longer notes can exist for a journalist, as long as the guest path stays short and ends on the menu or the table.

faqs.question: Where should the page send people?
faqs.answer: To the menu or the table for that specific restaurant. If the proof is about the private room, send them to the private inquiry, not the two-top widget. Name who the page is for, so the wrong night can opt out.

markdown:
A restaurant group case study page should show the constraint, the decision, and the room with one dish. A guest deciding where to go tonight is looking for a night they can picture, not a gallery. Photographs with no decision attached are decoration.

End the page on how a similar guest can see the menu or book a table. The proof is not finished when the last image is moody. It is finished when the next person knows which door to choose.

## The constraint before the steam

Open with the limit that made this room this room. Twelve seats and a kitchen that cannot do a la carte. A heritage dining room that cannot take a speaker. A lunch service that has to turn in forty minutes. A back room that used to be storage and still has one door. One constraint, in the first paragraph. A list of every hardship becomes a complaint. A single fact makes the dish make sense.

Write it the way you would brief a new host. Facts. If a reader cannot tell what was hard, the later photographs will be admired and forgotten. A pretty room without a limit looks like every other group's campaign.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) talks about showing how work was made, with evidence a reader can check, including photographs. A restaurant proof is that kind of account. The constraint is the test. The dish is the evidence. A screenshot of an empty booking grid, or a reel of uncaptioned plates, does not show how the night works.

Say what you were given. The shell of the building. The hours the street is busy. The decision not to open a fourth site. Readers trust a page that admits the starting point. A page that begins at the finished glow implies dinner arrived by taste alone.

## The decision, then the dish

After the constraint, one paragraph on the move. "We stopped a la carte at this address and serve a short set menu so the tiny kitchen can finish every plate." "We kept the front windows and put the louder bar in the back." The sentence should be repeatable. If a guest can retell it, the page worked.

Say what you refused when the refusal is the judgment. No birthday speeches in the small room. No separate vegan menu, because the set menu is already cooked that way on request. Refusal is often the proof. Guests who are judging whether the night fits them want to see that you can stop.

Then the dish. One plate that makes the decision visible. Not a collage. The leek, the chop, the bowl. Name it. Say which restaurant. Say whether it is on the menu this week. A proof page that will not name the food is still performing taste.

Credits for the architect, the photographer, and the builder of the fit-out can sit low. They do not replace the dish. A block of logos at the top tells a peer who was hired. It does not tell a guest where to eat.

## Photographs that carry the night

Choose frames that make the sentence visible. If the decision was twenty-four seats and no music, show the seats and the quiet, not a flash-lit crowd you staged once. If the decision was a dish that uses the whole animal, show that dish as it is served, not a raw ingredient in a mist.

Sequence the images in the order of the argument. The street, so they know the neighborhood. The room. The constraint, if it can be seen. The dish. Stop. Six frames tied to sentences teach more than thirty frames of linen.

Write the caption as part of the proof. "Holt Street, twenty-four seats, the grilled leek from the dinner menu" is a caption. "Interior" is not. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats images as content people need another way to perceive. Alt text should carry the fact: which room, what dish, what is happening. "Delicious food" fails the guest who can see, and it fails the guest who cannot.

Keep type in the page. Words burned into the photograph disappear for a reader and cannot be edited when the menu changes. The dish name will change. The caption has to be able to change with it.

Do not open on a logo animation or a title sequence. This page has a job. The job starts with the room.

## What a page without a decision is

A reel of hands, a map pin, and a list of suppliers is a lookbook. It can live on a social feed. It is a weak proof page, because a guest cannot tell what was difficult or whether they can book. A screenshot of the menu with no prices and no sentence has the same problem. The reader sees that a PDF exists. They do not see the night.

Cut images that do not change the argument. Two photographs of the same corner in different weather: keep the one that shows the seats. Empty beauty is decoration. The branch with hangers is a picture. It is not yet a restaurant.

Do not inflate the result. No invented covers, no invented waitlists, no quotes you do not have permission to print. A plain account of the constraint and the dish is stronger than a polished testimonial. If a guest will say a sentence in their own words and you may use it, keep it short and specific to the room.

Avoid a template so rigid that every restaurant pretends to have the same drama. Some rooms are quiet on purpose. Say so. Quiet and specific beats a false turning point about passion.

## End on a similar guest

The last block is the handoff. Name who this proof is for. "If you want the short set menu at Holt Street, see the menu and book a table. Parties larger than six belong on the private dining page." That sentence does more than a generic Reserve, because it sends the wrong guest away before the widget does.

Link to the matching restaurant, the menu, and one related room if the difference is useful. Three links. The reader should leave with a next step, not a maze of brand films.

Keep a single pair of labels, the same as the rest of the site. Menu. Book a table. If this proof is about a buyout, the label changes on purpose, and you say why. Do not invent a third verb for variety.

When you want a second pair of eyes on whether a page is proof or decoration, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring one restaurant you explain well at the table and the page that is supposed to explain it. The half hour should find the constraint, the dish, and the button. Hanabi designs and builds. The story has to stay true to service, because the floor will live with the promise.

## One room, told so a host could use it

Read the draft as if you are a host answering the phone. Could you point a guest at this page instead of repeating yourself? If not, the page is still an internal story. Add the fact you say every night. The room is loud. The menu is short. The kitchen closes at nine. Those facts feel unglamorous and they are the proof.

Include the practical line the photographs forget. How to get there, in one clause, not a map that fails. Whether the room suits a conversation or a celebration. The party size that still feels right. A guest deciding tonight is allowed to want romance and logistics in the same scroll. Give them both, in that order: the dish, then the fact that will save the booking.

Keep a before-and-after only when you changed the room and the change is the decision. The old storage door, the new pass. Two images and two sentences. A renovation diary with twenty dates is for the architect. The guest needs the result they will sit in.

If several restaurants share a proof template, lock the order and let the facts change. Constraint, decision, room, dish, menu, book. A template is a kindness when it forces the sentence. It is a failure when it forces every room to sound like the flagship. Write the sentence that would be false if you swapped the names. That is the one to keep.

Show the page to someone who has not eaten with you. Ask which restaurant it is, what they would order, and whether they would book for Saturday or for a quieter night. Their answer is the edit. If they say "it looks expensive" and you never stated the shape of the price, add one clause and a link to the menu where the numbers are. If they say "I do not know which suburb," the street fact is missing. Fix the missing fact before you add another frame of linen.

## How many proofs, and how a guest finds them

You do not need a case study for every special. You need one honest page per room that a stranger could use, plus a page for private dining if that is a real product. A new fit-out can get a proof when the constraint teaches something the homepage cannot hold. Old proofs that describe a menu you no longer cook should be updated or unpublished. A stale dish is a lie.

The guest who finishes one room needs a way to the other rooms, or back to booking, without decoding a poetic menu. Labels are the map. Restaurants, Menus, Book. Those are jobs.

That map is [navigation for a restaurant group](/blog/navigation-for-a-restaurant-group). Write the proof so it can be found by the guest it serves. A clear night buried under Explore still fails the person who was ready to book.
